speechtext:
Yes. Just before my hon. friend came in I was referring to an Ottawa Journal headline which reads "Western Tory in final criticism". However, I accept my hon. friend's objection to that word on a permanent basis.
Mr. Speaker, when I broke off at a quarter to six I think I had come to the point where I said it would appear that any decision we have made in the past with respect to a decision by Mr. Speaker has been made largely on party lines, and that probably any decision we may make in the future will be made largely on party lines. I repeated that I thought this situation was the result of the system we had in this country, and I did not criticize that system. I did submit to hon. members that they should consider whether or not we would ever avoid the possibility of that situation so long as we allowed an appeal to the house from a decision of Mr. Speaker.
In the course of this debate it has been implied-I do not think it has been suggested directly-that it is unfortunate that Mr. Speaker's conduct should be brought into question and that the matter could only be decided in this manner, namely by a resolution with respect to his conduct. Let me point out that this form of resolution could be used-I am not suggesting it is being so used at the moment-to advance the party disputes which occur in this house.
By one of the hon. members who spoke earlier in the debate I think it was suggested that the only way to resolve this problem was to dissolve the house so that we would have a new parliament and presumably a new Speaker. But let me point out that if an opposition felt that was the way to conduct the business of the house, and if they felt that a government would be obliged to dissolve parliament because they attacked the Speaker, then I suggest to you that these attacks might possibly be more frequent than they have been.

It is true that the government at least proposes to parliament the choice of a Speaker. That is the duty of the government. In this particular case I recall that the Leader of the Opposition joined in the recommendation to parliament. It would always be the duty of a government to recommend another Speaker on another occasion, whatever the government may be.
1 know that hon. members opposite feel extremely strongly on this particular point. I know that every one of them is aware of the great responsibility that all of us bear in the consideration of the discharge of the duties of Mr. Speaker. I am ready to agree that they must have given long, careful and serious thought to the proposal before us. Even if it were moved, as I think it was, at a time when feelings were stronger than they have been at any other time while I have been in the house, the fact of the matter is that the resolution was allowed to remain on the order paper and to be moved some 48 hours or so after that.
I give my hon. friends opposite full credit for taking a serious and solemn view of the problem before they engaged upon the debate of this resolution. But for the reasons I have given, Mr. Speaker, it would seem that it would lead to only one conclusion; and I wonder whether, under our system, any other conclusion could be reached and whether or not it is desirable that we should come to that conclusion.
May I just add one word more. Both the leader of the C.C.F. party and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, in their remarks, have spoken of the friendships they have enjoyed in the house, which they do not feel could continue under present conditions. I sincerely regret that expression of opinion. I have always had a high regard for both hon. members and for every other member of the opposition. I would hope we would recognize that if this motion is disposed of by a vote, it would be, generally speaking, on party lines; that is the only way, according to our rules, in which it could be disposed of.
For that reason I would hope that after this is over, all of us could take a view which would not be the view expressed by the two hon. gentlemen but rather that now we have discussed it and hon. members have expressed themselves-and I must say with dignity on every occasion-all of us could vote and accept the result; that we could take up where we left off without these friendships having been more than temporarily involved; and that we could once again work together in the sense that a government and an opposition work together in the larger sense of being part of a parliament which is here for
House of Commons
the purpose of disposing of the business of the people of Canada, with opposition, as my hon. friend has said, and with proposal and support on this side but on the basis-which is the true basis-that all of us are sent here to discharge our duties seriously and honestly, and that all of us are trying our very best to do that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. DREW-MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate with mixed feelings. So far as His Honour the Speaker is concerned I approach what I have to say with a heavy heart. So far as the government's part in this whole affair is concerned, it is difficult for me to express my feelings.
With regard to Mr. Speaker-though some may wonder at this in view of what has happened in the last few days and in view of what I may say before I take my seat-I am going to say that there is no friendship with any other person in this House of Commons that I value and enjoy more than 1 do my personal friendship with Mr. Speaker. So far as I am concerned that friendship arises because of my respect for his qualities as outlined this afternoon by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. I suppose it is also true to say that it arises because of a common interest in parliamentary procedure. Not only have I personal respect for my friend Rene Beaudoin, but I have the highest of regard for the industry with which he has applied himself to his task as Speaker and for the tremendous knowledge he has gained of parliamentary procedure across the centuries. Despite what has happened in the last few days and despite what duty compels me to do in this debate, I hope that friendship between us will continue.
When I think of Mr. Speaker and what he has done for parliament in these last three years-up until a few days ago-I am conscious of the job he has done here on the floor of parliament. I say this to the Minister of Finance, despite the specious attempt he made to picture the opposition as having been critical of Mr. Speaker for a long time. I say that Mr. Speaker's job in this parliament has been appreciated by all of us in the opposition just as much as by those who sit to his right.

speechtext:
I thank the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration for confirming that fact. First may I say that there were no appeals in the session of 1954. In the session of 1955, there was only one appeal. It occurred on July 5 of that year and is recorded on pages 5683, 5684 and 5685 of Hansard. The appeal was made by the Progressive Conservatives. When the vote was called naturally the Progressive Conservatives voted against Mr. Speaker's ruling but we of the C.C.F., along with the members of the Social Credit party and the members of the government, voted to sustain Mr. Speaker's ruling. Let the record speak for itself, Mr. Speaker. Prior to the pipe-line debate there were only two appeals of Speaker's rulings in this parliament. In one case we voted against the ruling and on one occasion we voted to sustain the ruling.
The other of the two to which I have referred occurred on March 23 of this year, and is recorded on page 2457 of Hansard. The occasion was a motion for the production of papers moved by my colleague the hon. member for Yorkton to which the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration applied a treatment that was dug out of antiquity. We did not like it. We protested against it and we argued about it. At this moment I cannot recall whether we were thinking of appealing the ruling, but in the course of the argument Mr. Speaker was offended by something the hon. member for Prince Albert said and the result was that Mr. Speaker virtually challenged the hon. member for Prince Albert to appeal the ruling. The hon. member for Prince Albert did so, and that was the occasion when we voted against Mr. Speaker's ruling.

In addition to the fact that for two and a half sessions there were only two appeals, there have been quite a number of occasions when Mr. Speaker has ruled against motions or amendments moved from this side of the house. I confess that the number of rulings against motions or amendments made by members of the C.C.F. group seems to be fewer than is the case for members to my right or left, but there have been some cases affecting all three parties on this side of the house. In none of those other cases except the two to which I have referred were appeals launched. I call my colleagues around me as witnesses to this statement. There have been several occasions when one colleague or another has been dissatisfied with the ruling Mr. Speaker has made and has suggested to me that I should appeal it. I have turned around and said, "No; Mr. Speaker is being fair." There have been occasions when Mr. Speaker has ruled against the government. He ruled against the Minister of Finance in respect of the Post Office Act. So I have said to my colleagues, Mr. Speaker is being fair and if we like his rulings when he rules against the government we cannot stand up and appeal his rulings when he rules against us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
So far as we are concerned, it does not matter. The occupants of the chair are one; and whichever occupant has made a ruling we have been happy, until the start of the pipe-line debate, over the kind of impartial treatment given to this House of Commons by the occupants of the chair during this twenty-second parliament.
I confess that in the parliament from 1945 to 1949 we got into the habit of making appeals. There was no other way we could get a vote. Those who were here remember the experience. Perhaps it was because we made so many appeals from 1945 to 1949 that the habit carried over into the next parliament for a time, but we soon discovered that in Mr. Speaker Macdonald we had a presiding officer in whom we could place our confidence. In fact, I remember that once in the very early months of his Speakership he ruled against the Prime Minister, and the habit of making appeals began to disappear. The habit had virtually died out with Mr. Speaker Macdonald, and when Mr. Speaker Beaudoin came into the chair he inherited a happy relationship between the house and the Chair and he was able to develop that relationship into one of the best relationships that could ever have obtained between the Speaker and the House of Commons.

I know that I enjoyed it. I know that the friendships built up during that period are such that, so far as I am concerned, they will outlast even the experience through which we are going now. I repeat that the conduct of the Speaker up until a short while ago was something that deserves from all of us the highest commendation.
I am conscious, Mr. Speaker, not only of the tremendous job you have done here in the house. I am conscious not only of your impartiality across the years to us here in this chamber, but I also have very vivid memories of a committee over which Mr. Speaker presided for two full sessions. I refer to the committee which was set up for the purpose of revising the rules of the house, which brought in a report that was adopted last July, a report which in due course became our standing orders as they are now constituted. I say to the Minister of Finance, and he knows this, that if it had not been for the approach of Mr. Speaker, if it had not been for his impartiality; if it had not been for his determination that the rules of this parliament were to be the rules of parliament and not the rules of the majority, there would not have been a unanimous report last summer.
My friend the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre is confirming that statement. The Minister of Finance knows that after two years of battling things out in that committee, that was subsequent to earlier committees in the days of Mr. Speaker Macdonald, and Mr .Speaker Fauteux, finally the point was reached in that committee where we were at loggerheads. We could not agree. The Minister of Finance had his rule changes that he felt the committee should adopt. We had gone through them; we had argued them; we had voted and we had had amendments. We had spent all kinds of hours without reaching a report that could be unanimous at all.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, the hon. member for Kamloops, the hon. member for Acadia, the Minister of Finance and others who were members of that committee will recall that things were getting difficult.	It looked as though the
battle was lost. It looked as though the Minister of Finance was going to get his way simply by moving that the changes the government wanted be put through, that the report be made back to the house and put through by a majority vote of the House of Commons.
What did Mr. Speaker do? The minister knows what he did. He said he would not present to the House of Commons in his name as chairman a report that was the report of
House of Commons
the majority only. There had to be compromise; there had to be a report that would represent as nearly as possible unanimity of opinion on the part of that committee, and I remember the night across the way in room 16 when Mr. Speaker almost literally took four heads and banged them together, the head of the Minister of Finance, the head of the hon. member for Kamloops, the head of the hon. member for Acadia and my head. He said, "It is time for you four fellows to get out and get together in a subcommittee and come back with a report".
The proposal of Mr. Speaker became a motion and a decision of the committee was reached late that night, at eleven o'clock or perhaps twelve o'clock, in room 16 across the way. As instructed we were up in the office of the Minister of Finance on the fourth floor at nine o'clock the next morning. We started in, and my colleagues will confirm if, and found it was tough going, particularly under those circumstances, to try to give and take, but we did it.
I was looking today at Hansard of July 1, 1955, when the report of that committee was moved in this house by the Minister of Finance and seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops. But for the fact that the hon. member for Kamloops was seen first, either one of the other two of us would have had the honour to second it. Why? Because we had reached unanimity, because we had a presiding officer in this house who sensed what parliament should be like, who insisted that the rules of parliament were the rules of parliament, not the rules of the government; and this book we have, or this book we had until a week ago, the standing orders of the House of Commons, representing the unanimous report of the committee that worked for years, is our possession in the House of Commons because of the impartiality, because of the fairness, because of the appreciation of parliamentary tradition in the heart and mind of Mr. Speaker Louis Rene Beaudoin.
I shall never forget that experience. No matter what comes out of this situation in which we are, my friendship for him, my regard for him will continue. But, Mr. Speaker, in the meantime something has happened. First may I say, indicating our continuing regard for Mr. Speaker, indicating also the attitude of this house toward Mr. Speaker's rulings, that as late as May 3 of this year when the fever of the pipe line was beginning to rise though the legislation had not yet reached us, there was a motion under standing order 26 moved by the Leader of the Opposition that had to do with a pretty contentious issue,

House of Commons
the McMahon correspondence, and some question as to whether the Minister of Trade and Commerce had been completely fair with the house.
Mr. Speaker ruled the motion of the Leader of the Opposition out of order. The Leader of the Opposition appealed the ruling. It was one of those cases where no appeal is allowed. Mr. Speaker, in his desire to be fair, was leaning over backward. If you read Hansard of that day, May 3, 1956,-most members do not have to read it; it is still fresh enough in our memories-you will see that the point was reached where it looked as though Mr. Speaker was going to allow an appeal. Who was it that came to his support; who was it that rallied Mr. Speaker to stand firm; who was it that reminded him of his previous decisions? It was my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. Supported by the statement my leader gave on that occasion, Mr. Speaker rallied and refused the appeal that the Leader of the Opposition sought to make. There the matter rested. That is the kind of regard this house had for Mr. Speaker until recent days.
I come down to May 7 of this year, the day before that dramatic day when the Liberals held a caucus in the morning and the Minister of Trade and Commerce made his statement in the afternoon and filed notice before six o'clock of the resolution preceding Bill No. 298. My leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, presented a motion to adjourn the house under standing order 26 to discuss the matter of an across-Canada pipe line, with the suggestion of public ownership in the motion. This was something pretty basic and pretty fundamental so far as we were concerned.
It was ruled out of order by Mr. Speaker. In his comments he said something which we thought indicated that he was prepared to have an appeal. My leader asked whether that was what he meant. Mr. Speaker said, "No, there is no appeal". My leader accepted it. It ended there. This was on the day before the Minister of Trade and Commerce stood in this house and told parliament what it was he was going to demand, no matter what it might do to parliament, as we have learned to our sorrow. That is the kind of Speaker we had until recent days; that is the kind of relationship we had between the Chair and the members of this house. Then came the determination of that minister who operates on the slogan, "What Lola wants, Lola gets", and there followed the days which are now part of bitter memory.
I am not going through the things that happened during the first few days of that debate when we began to feel that something had happened, something had snapped. But

that was our experience. Where was our Speaker, where was the man in whom we had learned to place such confidence? Point after point that we would raise was turned down. We fell back on our only recourse, that of making appeals. The more we felt we were being denied our rights, particularly under the threat of closure, the more it seemed as though there was nothing else for us to do but to keep on raising points of procedure, trying to establish and to protect our rights.
Finally came the day that caused all the trouble. I shall not discuss anything that happened previous to May 31 and June 1, because up to that point I think we might have survived; although, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway pointed out, he warned the house and the government a few days before that we were drifting toward a crisis.
Well, other members have recited what happened on the night of May 31 when Mr. Speaker, after having heard the point of order of my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, heard the point of privilege made by my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo, and suggested to him that he should not proceed with the point of privilege unless he was prepared to put it in the form of a motion. He did so; he followed the instructions of Mr. Speaker as to how to draft the motion. He sent the documents in question to the Clerk, as suggested by Mr. Speaker. Everything was being done just as Mr. Speaker was suggesting that it be done. The next morning, June 1, something seemed to have happened. The Winnipeg Free Press in an editorial on Monday, June 4, 1956, said this:
The circumstances may, for once, be fairly put in an analogy with a football game. Late in the third quarter, the referee makes a decision that leads on to a vital score for the visiting side. The officials of the home team are obviously much upset. The fourth quarter begins with the referee announcing that he has changed his mind, that he made a wrong decision in the third quarter, and therefore play shall now proceed from where it was before he made that decision.
How apt is that description.

subtopic: MR. DREW-MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: I'll say.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MR. DREW-MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
That morning, June 1, our trusted and revered Mr. Speaker, the one in whom we had such confidence, began to break standing orders and citations right and left. I ask you first of all to note citation 216 in Beauchesne's third edition:
On resuming an adjourned debate, the member who moved its adjournment is by courtesy entitled to speak first if he rises in his place when the order is called.

I ask you to couple that with standing order 7, which the Prime Minister quoted to us the other day in another debate, which reads:
At the ordinary time of adjournment of the house, unless otherwise provided, the proceedings shall be interrupted and the business under consideration at the termination of the sitting shall stand over until the next sitting day when it will be taken up at the same stage where its progress was interrupted.
It is clearly established that on the morning of June 1 the Leader of the Opposition had the floor; he was in the middle of his speech. Interrupting him at that point was a violation of standing order 7 and a discourtesy to the Leader of the Opposition under citation 216 of Beauchesne's third edition. "But oh", says someone, "it is proper for the Speaker at that point if he feels he must do so to raise a point of order". No. In doing that Mr. Speaker violated the provisions of standing order 50, which reads:
Whenever Mr. Speaker is of opinion that a motion offered to the house is contrary to the rules and privileges of parliament, he shall apprise the house thereof immediately, before putting the question thereon, and quote the standing order or authority applicable to the case.
If the motion of my friend the hon. member for Nanaimo was out of order, the time for Mr. Speaker to tell the house was before he put the question. But no; the night before he put the question as in order. Rising on a point of order discourteously in the midst of the speech of the Leader of the Opposition I say was out of order. Then Mr. Speaker refused to hear anyone on his point of order. His contention was that this motion which was in order the night before was out of order the next morning.
I shall not go into the argument as to whether any of the rest of us might also have had the right to speak to the point of order; if that were at stake I would argue that too, but I am not going to confuse it by going that far. But I do say this, that in addition to the standing orders and citations I have already given which our revered and trusted Mr. Speaker broke, he on that occasion broke standing order 34, which reads as follows:
Any member addressing the house, if called to order either by Mr. Speaker or on a point raised by another member, shall sit down while the point is being stated, after which he may explain.
The Leader of the Opposition sat down and Mr. Speaker stated his point of order but he denied the Leader of the Opposition the right to explain after he had sat down. What a way to start a day, a day we shall never forget.
Now, of course, we have had the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance indulge 67509-306
House of Commons
in what I can only call distortion, because they have tried to contend that Mr. Speaker forecast the night before the ruling against the motion which he made the morning of June 1. I apologize to the house for the anger with which I interrupted the Minister of Finance this afternoon, but I confess that is how I felt. Perhaps I should not have made the apology.
The Minister of Finance this afternoon endeavoured to create the impression that the ruling Mr. Speaker gave on the morning of June 1 was not something new but something forecast by what was said the night before. The minister tried to create that impression in two ways. On the one hand he drew attention to his own intervention in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition, recorded at page 4531 of Hansard, when he suggested that no motion of any kind should have been entertained by the Speaker at that time.
Mr. Speaker did not rule the motion out of order the next morning on that ground; not at all. I say it is unfair, it is misleading the house and it is a case of distortion for the Minister of Finance to try to say that his intervention here in the house the night before was the basis upon which Mr. Speaker made his ruling the next morning. Then in an attempt to create the impression that some doubt had been cast the night before on the validity of my hon. friend's motion, the Minister of Finance read this, quoting from Mr. Speaker's words as recorded at page 4532 of Hansard:
This is a matter on which perhaps I might give a ruling on a future occasion-
It was at that point I burst in saying that it was shameful for the Minister of Finance to mislead the house in that way, trying to suggest that Mr. Speaker the night before had said to the house that he might have to rule the next day on the whole motion.

This is what represents the real problem, because next morning we had a complete turnabout. There was an attempt by the Prime Minister like that of the Minister of Finance. I mention the Prime Minister because he did the same thing as the Minister of Finance when he spoke on Monday, June 4, where he is reported at page 4655 of Hansard as follows:
You had already made it quite clear that you felt you might have to make a ruling upon the question at some time. On the following morning, when the matter was called, you did give the ruling that was cited in the Votes and Proceedings of June 1 by the Leader of the Opposition.

In addition we have this business of submitting a proposition to the house by Mr. Speaker for a majority decision. That has been discussed at great length, so I need not argue about it in theoretical or abstract terms. I am going to read some standing orders to show just how wrong this was. Standing order 41 reads:
Forty-eight hours' notice shall be given of a motion for leave to present a bill, resolution or
House of Commons
address, for the appointment of any committee, or for placing a question on the order paper; but this rule shall not apply to bills after their introduction, or to private bills, or to the times of meeting or adjournment of the house. Such notice shall be laid on the table before six o'clock p.m., and be printed in the Votes and Proceedings of that day.
That is a standing order which requires notices for certain kinds of motions and it permits certain exceptions, but what the Speaker put to the house was not one of those exceptions. What the Speaker put to the house might be regarded as coming under standing order 42, which reads:

subtopic: MR. DREW-MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as every other speaker who has taken part in this debate has said, it is an unpleasant experience which we are undergoing. It certainly is one in which no one participates with any degree of pleasure or satisfaction because I can say, as was said by the last speaker and by every other hon. gentleman, I think, who has taken part in this debate, that I have had the highest regard for Mr. Speaker and the other occupants of the chair coming under that title, and also a personal regard and a warm friendship as well. Therefore it is particularly unfortunate that we are faced, as we believe, with the necessity and the responsibility for proceeding with this matter at this time.
It perhaps would be a relatively easy thing to sit in one's seat and not take part in the debate, but because I feel strongly on this matter, because I feel that hon. members have a duty which has to be performed in this connection, I do not think any one of us should remain seated and hide behind someone else who is undertaking this responsibility and performing this task at this time. So, much as I regret it personally, I feel that I have a responsibility here as a member of parliament, as a member of the opposition, and I am exercising it tonight, though I certainly agree with many of the things which have been said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre

about His Honour the Speaker, and the personal relationships which have existed heretofore between us.
There is another reason why I rise to take part in this debate. I must say that I was somewhat shocked by the statement of the Prime Minister when he spoke in connection with this motion on Monday, June 4. The right hon. gentleman, after referring to the motion and quoting from an editorial, went on to say this about our action, as found at page 4654 of Hansard:
Not because of the qualities of the Speaker or the chairman but because of the fact that there is a contentious measure that is being opposed by all means that can be devised under the rules of the house to bring about delay and to waste time.
Again on page 4657 the Prime Minister said in a tone, I say with respect, of deepest sarcasm:
This situation will appear to many, in spite of the elevated tone of the addresses made in the house this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition and by the leader of the C.C.F. party, as being one more attempt to prevent the majority in parliament from reaching a point where it would be entitled to vote upon the propriety or otherwise of this controversial measure.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that I for one resent the imputations which are contained in these two statements of the Prime Minister, and I regret that the Prime Minister has shown so little appreciation of the sense of this house and the sincerity of the feelings which have been aroused by the matters which have gone on during the past week that he would suggest that we would move this motion simply for the purpose of bringing about delay. All the irritations, all the frustrations which have occurred during the preceding weeks undoubtedly contributed to an unhealthy atmosphere, undoubtedly caused irritations on our side of the house as well, but those irritations in themselves would never have prompted this motion had it not been for the matters to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred a few minutes ago.
It was when we finally came to what I am afraid will go down in parliamentary history as black Friday that we were confronted with a situation where we felt that there was nothing else that could be done. When you see, Mr. Speaker, as you and others undoubtedly did, and as hon. members have indicated, reasonable men, experienced parliamentarians, some of whom have been here for almost a quarter of a century, so angered, so aroused that they had to use means which had never been used before in the Canadian parliament, you can judge to some extent of the intensity of the feelings of the members and the sincerity of the

feelings of the members of the opposition and of the Leader of the Opposition when he gave notice of this motion.
To suggest that we would impute, charge and indict an officer for whom so many have had the warmest personal feelings, one who personified within himself all the respect which is due the Chair; to suggest we would do that for partisan purposes is an implication which I resent, and that is one reason I am speaking on this motion tonight. Certainly, sir, if notice of this motion had been given for any of these purposes or there had been any suggestion of them I certainly would not be speaking at this time.
Then there is another reason why we are perhaps all the more interested in this now than we would have been heretofore. That is because of some of the academic discussions which have also arisen, and the suggestions as to the rights of the majority and of the minorities. No one questions the fact that a majority represented by the government has the responsibility for initiating legislation and seeing that it is properly debated in parliament, because parliament is the forum wherein that debate takes place, where public opinion is formulated, crystallized and so on and so forth.
But although one can appreciate the general philosophy, the general principle, that a majority cannot be continually obstructed or blocked by a minority, that proposition made in general certainly has no application whatsoever in the situation which developed here. If one wants authority for that one could refer, for instance, to an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press which deals with this question of discussion of the rights of a majority and the rights of a minority. This is what the Winnipeg Free Press says:
The government has struggled for years with the pipe line problem.	Mr. Howe has made
decisions, found that they did not work, and made new decisions .	. . Eventually out of all
this confusion, there comes a bill. And Mr. Howe says, in effect: "Right, we've decided what's best for the country; time is short; whisk it through."
There is here something dangerously near the idea that the government's thinking is enough, and that parliament's argument in public, as the focus for popular thought and discussion, does not matter.
If one wants a further illustration of the working of democracy and the function of debate, I would recommend that the Secretary of State for External Affairs see that his book is properly distributed to the members on his own side of the house. One could take his book, "Democracy in World Politics" and occupy a lot of time tonight putting most interesting quotations on the record as to the functions of debate in parliament, the rights of an opposition to debate; how it
House of Commons
eliminates the dark corners, helps to crystallize public opinion and even reaches over the shoulders of a majority. I see the minister has the book in his hand. I am sure he would be glad to have many copies of it sold, and I hope that tonight he will perhaps reread it and then read the speech he made the other night and try to reconcile what he said in the book with what he said in the House of Commons as to the functions of an opposition and a majority in this parliament.
Dealing with this matter, I should like to call the attention of that distinguished former president of the Canadian Bar Association, the Prime Minister, to a statement of principle laid down by the Canadian Bar Association a few years ago, when they said:
Under democratic institutions, the people accept to be governed by majority decisions, but on condition that the laws should be discussed in the open, traversed by the criticisms of the opposition and be the result of a free and enlightened decision of parliament.
I wonder how much discussion there is when the motion is that further consideration be postponed? How much discussion is there when the Leader of the Opposition, rising time after time to speak on a matter, is refused recognition by the occupant of the chair at that time, in violation of all the ancient usages and principles of this house and of other parliamentary houses?
Never before was such a spectacle seen. On four different occasions the Leader of the Opposition stood in his place, as he had a right to do, and with respect, and the Chair should have recognized him. But each time the Chair refused to recognize him. Despite all this-I say despite these irritations, despite these frustrations, despite the intensity of feeling which was engendered-this motion would not have been made had it not been for what happened on that Friday morning.
I am not going to deal with that matter in detail. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has outlined it substantially in so far as precedents and citations are concerned. May I just go back before that for a moment. If we accept this matter to which I referred a moment ago, namely the fact of the relative importance of the position of the majority in comparison with that of the minority, I suggest we are going back to the principles which prevailed 500 years ago when parliament consisted of the king's men, with the pocket boroughs and all the rest, and when the executive were in the king's pocket. It was against that arbitrary rule that we finally developed through the centuries these principles which were incorporated in this book to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred a while

House of Commons
ago. I refer to our standing orders, our rules and all the citations which preceded them. That was what evolved through the centuries.
Where are we now? As has been pointed out, because of what happened on Friday morning, in a very few minutes all of this which had happened before was scrapped and apparently thrown out the window. The Leader of the Opposition, on rising to continue a speech he had started the night before in a debate which had been adjourned in the regular way, was knocked down almost as quickly as if he had been pole-axed. He was stopped dead and ordered to sit down. He was given no opportunity to speak; he was given no opportunity to continue the debate. He was refused that right. He was even refused the right to raise a point of order and he was told by Mr. Speaker, "You have your remedy; you can appeal".
We listened to the Minister of Finance this afternoon in a long, technical, legalistic argument which I am afraid did not go too far toward defence of the Chair, Mr. Speaker, but which perhaps at least put the Minister of Finance on record as having intervened in some way in this matter by a speech. What did the Minister of Finance say this afternoon? What was the whole motive and theme of his statement? It was that these appeals from the Speaker's rulings are always political, and everyone knows they are political. He said it was unfortunate that was the case but that you had to have these political decisions; and he was almost suggesting and hoping that perhaps some day we would be able to obviate the necessity for appeals from Speakers' rulings; that is, purely political appeals.
Then I would refer you to the statement of Mr. Speaker on Friday morning, as recorded at page 4542 of Hansard, when refusing the Leader of the Opposition the right to speak. He went on to say this:
... I propose not to make a ruling but to submit this position to the judgment of the house. If the house decides in favour of it, then we shall govern ourselves accordingly.
Then later on he said to the Leader of the Opposition, "You have your right; you can appeal to the house". What right was there? What justification was there, Mr. Speaker, for stopping that debate when it was stopped and for refusing to give the Leader of the Opposition even a chance to be heard?
Then later on we had that other unprecedented move that was made, this formulation of a proposition or submission to the house by the Speaker in which he attempted to reverse himself and take us back 24 hours into the previous day instead of having the

debate carried on in the way in which it should have been carried on. At page 4552 of Hansard I notice that it is put in the form of a motion: "Those who are in favour of this motion, will please say yea". Who made the motion, Mr. Speaker? Certainly not Mr. Speaker. Certainly no one on the government side of the house.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration was very vociferous tonight in his defence of Mr. Speaker by interjection; but I did not notice any of them rising at any time when these discussions were on to help Mr. Speaker. I did not notice any of them answering points of order. As someone has said, Mr. Speaker had to carry the whole load himself. They sat back and allowed him to do it, or at least they did not help Mr. Speaker in any way.

subtopic: MR. DREW-MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no objection to my hon. friend asking a question, but as I said a moment ago he has been very reluctant to get into this debate so far. I certainly do not want him to be deprived of that privilege, but I do not want him to make a speech in the middle of mine. Later on he will have an opportunity to speak if he desires to take advantage of it.
I was referring a moment ago to the fact that at page 4552 you have the usual phrasing or phraseology but it is most unusual having regard to the background: "Those who are in favour of this motion will please say yea". No motion had been made whatsoever. So we had that situation, namely that in one short morning Mr. Speaker had reversed himself with regard to what he had done the night before; he had refused debate; he made a submission from the Chair which, with deference, I suggest was unwarranted and submitted it; and then he set the clock back 24 hours.
I think it can be summed up in one way, Mr. Speaker. For some reason Mr. Speaker acted as a wrecking crew to get back on the

rails the government locomotive which had been so effectively derailed the night before, and without his intervention it never could have been put back on the rails. That is what happened. It was then, and only then, that we saw in the house the scenes which took place and to which reference has been made in the press time and time again. It was after that had occurred that the Leader of the Opposition gave notice of this motion, which the Prime Minister said was made for the purpose of delaying debate. I say that it was not made for that reason in any way shape or form.
Much has been said about intervention. I listened very carefully to the Minister of Finance who spoke this afternoon. As I said, he gave a refined, legalistic argument about the rules of the House of Commons. I noticed that there were some things with which he did not deal. I know that my hon. friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs must have read with a great deal of interest the comments which have appeared in the press lately, and particularly the editorial comments of a gentleman named Mr. Norman Smith who is a liberal certainly with a small "1" if not with a capital "L". He is one who sat here and observed these proceedings. He is well known to some hon. gentlemen opposite and is a personal friend of many. Certainly he could never be accused of making any political capital for the Conservative party. But as a disinterested observer, as a man who has travelled the world over and seen some of the scenes of disorder, some of the dissolutions of parliaments to which the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred the other evening, and who has travelled with him, what does he say about the events of Friday morning. He says the Liberal party tore up the rule book, and not only tore up the rule book but part of his national pride in citizenship. Moreover, they went about their tasks with a gladsome thumping of desks. Certainly, Mr. Speaker is not responsible for the thumping of desks, but that epitomizes the situation just about as succinctly, just as about as fairly as anything that could be said.
There are many things that could be read from these articles which would be very unkind. I do not want to put them on the record. Mr. Smith goes out of his way to say, and it is certainly true, that these gentlemen are not fascists; they are not commun-nists. He said they are just ignorant, and ignorance was the kindest thing that could be said about them. I think probably that is about as fair an observation as could be made. In his column Mr. Smith also goes on to say-it is unfortunate the Minister of Finance did not deal with this point this afternoon-
House of Commons
that there were notes passing back and forth between the government leader and Mr. Speaker. Sometimes other cabinet ministers were used as office boys. Finally, when the notes were intercepted, the house leader became more astute and went out into the lobby to pick up the notes carried back and forth.
Those are the facts as set forth by Mr. Norman Smith. I was hoping that this afternoon the Minister of Finance would give some explanation or stand up, as the hon. member for Kamloops did a while ago, and deny them very pointedly. No; we heard long appeals about fairness in a political situation such as this, but certainly nothing which went to any of these matters that have been referred to in the local newspapers printed here in Ottawa and which have certainly come to the attention of all who were involved in the situation. Certainly, I thought they would have been dealt with this afternoon.

speechtext: No; make your speech afterwards. You will have plenty of time. At least, Mr. Speaker, in fairness to the chair these things should be dealt with; they should be explained. At least this could be said for King James when he came into the House of Commons; he took control of the chair and threw the Speaker out of it. He did not skulk behind the chair, and that is more than a suggestion of what has gone on around this place.

speechtext: What king did you say?

subtopic: MR. DREW-MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
King James; but you have a better knowledge of history than I and perhaps it was Charles, at any rate one of the Stuarts. It was three hundred years ago. I can understand why the minister would be a better authority than I am because the government is repeating the same procedure that was carried on in those days. He probably made a study of the technique that was used, but I say at least the Stuarts took over the chair. I have even heard the remark that once in this house when the chairman was refusing to "see" an hon. member, some hon. member was so exasperated he may have gone up and twisted the chairman's head around and said, "Now can you see him?" But at any rate neither he nor the Stuart king skulked behind the chair.
At any rate, there were those events of black Friday for which there has been no explanation. We all know that Mr. Speaker was under tremendous difficulty. We know he was tired. We know he had been sitting in that chair under a terriffic strain. We recognize all those things, and the same would apply of course to his assistants, the deputy

House of Commons
and the deputy chairman. However, that does not explain what happened; that cannot explain this reversal which took place on Friday morning.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the Minister of Finance talk about his great qualities, his experience, his personality, none of which is denied. This makes it all the more difficult to understand why he acted the way he did on Friday morning. A less experienced man, one who had made many mistakes before, one who was not conversant with the rules, one who was not a thorough gentleman, could have been expected to crack up under the pressure of some of the things which were done. It is because of that complete reversal, because of this background that suggestions, call them innuendoes if you like, have been made deliberately in the press as to what has gone on; and yet no explanation has been given.
It is a good thing, Mr. Speaker, to have this motion before us. We regret the necessity for it, but it was time it was dealt with. It had to be dealt with. Parliament could not continue, and how it is going to continue I do not know. A while ago the Minister of Finance said he hoped that after this was disposed of personal friendships could be restored. I hope so too. Personal friendships are something which we all value. One of the great traditions of our parliamentary system is that we do not allow the acrimony of debate on public matters to interfere with personal relationships and personal friendships. But personal friendships be as they may, the fact remains that parliament cannot carry on unless there is implicit confidence in the Chair, its impartiality and its independence of the executive. This confidence has gone. I say with all the seriousness which I can command, Mr. Speaker, that confidence cannot be restored in this parliament. There is only one way.
Someone suggested a while ago, and I thought it was another innuendo, that perhaps we were bringing this on to force an election. We are certainly not bringing this on to force an election. There are other ways if we wanted to do that which could perhaps be explored. I do say that although this certainly was not brought on with any such intention, the root problem will not be solved until after an election, until after a new government and a new house have come back and new officials have been elected. Then perhaps we can start to rebuild and repair the damage which was done during the last few days.
As has been said by so many others more effectively than I can say it, it is not a matter

of the ruling on Friday; it is not the special damage which may have been done to one party or the assistance which may have been given to another, serious as those things may be, but the fact that these are part of the precedents of the House of Commons. They have become part of the fabric and will become interwoven into our parliamentary procedure.
They cannot be allowed to exist in that way, Mr. Speaker. Something will have to be done under a new parliament to eradicate these things and restore the prestige of the Chair. It is for that reason we feel as strongly as we do, and why I am speaking on this motion tonight. It is parliament, the institution which we have revered, which we respect and which the thousands of people who were lining up trying to get into the galleries revered and respected as well. It is indeed woven into the warp and woof of our being, and damage has been done to it-I was going to say almost irreparable damage. It is irreparable under the existing circumstances. I think it can be rectified in time, but it is a matter which must be dealt with by this house.
A partisan vote may be necessary. I quite appreciate, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway said this afternoon, that may be the result. I have no illusions, either, as to the result of this vote, but it will be recorded in Hansard that the opposition has stood up and protected what it sincerely believed to be the rights of parliament. The opposition has gone further than any one individual would have gone to preserve those rights, and that will probably be the most healthy precedent of all which will come out of this turmoil and trouble of the past few weeks.

subtopic: MR. DREW-MOTION OF NON-CONFIDENCE IN PRESIDING OFFICER OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me trace the history of the motion that has been under discussion tonight in order to put the record straight in some aspects of the distortions that have been made of the proceedings. You will recall, sir, that when I rose on a question of privilege I was instructed by Mr. Speaker that it would be necessary for me to follow a certain procedure if I wished to pursue the matter. He outlined that procedure to me and I followed it. It included the drafting of a motion, the finding of an hon. member to second it, and sending the motion to the Speaker in the chair.
There has been the suggestion here this evening that Mr. Speaker was in doubt at that time as to whether the motion was in order; that he had in fact almost decided

House of Commons
on the Thursday night that on Friday he would have to rule it out of order. I can well understand why my hon. friends in the cabinet should wish to convey that impression; but I suggest to you, sir, that it is a continuation of the cruel and callous treatment which that cabinet has meted out to the Speaker of this house. It is a determination that he shall be made the goat all the way down.
I am going to quote from page 4532 of Hansard to show that Mr. Speaker not only had no doubt that it was in order but so indicated to the house at that time, because he interrupted the Leader of the Opposition when he was speaking with these words:
Order. I intervene at this moment to indicate to the Leader of the Opposition that in debating this matter one cannot go beyond what is considered privilege. In this article which I have just read it is my view that what may be called privilege in the letter written by Miss Marjorie Le Lacheur is the last paragraph:
"It means nothing to them that debate in the house has long been a farce, with the cat-calls and jeers of the Liberals, and the systematic garroting of the opposition by Mr. Speaker ..." These are the words:
"... and the systematic garroting of the opposition by Mr. Speaker, making a mockery of this democracy for which so many of their fathers have died."
The words that are privilege are "the systematic garroting of the opposition by Mr. Speaker". All the other words are not privilege.
Then the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar raised the question at that point as to whether the narrowing of the points of privilege suggested by the Speaker was in fact correct and suggested that it was more or less an attack on the whole house. Following that, Mr. Speaker reiterated his position and in the paragraph the Minister of Finance did not read this afternoon Mr. Speaker said this:
I am under the impression-and I am sure the hon. member upon reflection will agree with me- that, freedom of the press being what it is, freedom of expression outside this parliament and the right of criticising whatever takes place here being what it is, no one on a question of privilege should object to the first two paragraphs and, even in the third paragraph, no one should object to anything if there were not those few words, in which the Speaker is accused of a systematic garroting of the opposition. As far as the other paragraphs are concerned, I see no privilege at all in them.
Now, there is the clear statement of the Speaker of this house that he recognized that my motion was in order the night before, and any contention now on the part of members of the cabinet that he had already half made up his mind to rule it out of order is a gross distortion of Mr. Speaker's expressed views on the evening of Thursday, May 31. When he ruled it out of order on Friday, June 1, he did not actually rule on the question as to whether or not my motion was in order. I had 
brought a motion before the house. Mr. Speaker ruled not whether my motion was in order but whether the charges contained in the motion were sustainable. When he reversed his decision of the night before I was faced with the question as to what had induced him to do so, and I could think of only three alternatives.
The first was that my motion was actually out of order, that Mr. Speaker had been mistaken, that his knowledge and understanding of the rules of procedure had not been adequate to make a decision as to whether or not my motion was in order. After all that has been said on all sides of the house both this afternoon and on previous occasions when this matter has been discussed, no hon. member will seriously contend that the Speaker of this house is not competent to decide whether or not a motion is in order. We have had very lengthy eulogies concerning his vast fund of knowledge of parliamentary procedure. It has been stated that with the possible exception of one Speaker our present Speaker stands head and shoulders above the usual speakers of the Canadian House of Commons in possessing an exhaustive knowledge of the rules of procedure.
I think we have to throw that suggestion out. Mr. Speaker at that time knew this motion was in order; he was not just guessing, he knew it and he expressed to the house, as I have shown quite clearly, his reasons for thinking it was in order.
That brings me to my next possible alternative for his extraordinary action on the morning of Friday, June 1; and that is that Mr. Speaker maliciously and deliberately gave me wrong advice with the intention of ruling it out of order at a later date. That also is a proposition to which I cannot subscribe; it goes against all the past record of Mr. Speaker. Not only that, it cannot be sustained when one places it alongside Mr. Speaker's reactions not only on this occasion but on a previous occasion when I raised a similar question of privilege with regard to an editorial appearing in a Montreal newspaper. On both those occasions Mr. Speaker expressed himself as gravely concerned over the seriousness of these situations. In fact when the much publicized attempt of the Minister of Finance to raise a point of order on this particular motion was brought to the attention of the house Mr. Speaker had this to say:
The matter raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) is one of privilege and is one that is very serious. I had not seen the letter entitled "They Will Pay" but I had read the letter written by Mr. Eugene Forsey, in which he discusses instances in which I was myself involved. It would seem to me, however, that in a matter of this kind the thing to do, after

having placed ourselves in a position where we can deal with the matter, especially since I am concerned, is to postpone the consideration of that motion.
Now it is true he suggested postponement of it, but he also referred to our having placed ourselves in a position where we could do something about it. The reference very clearly is to a motion which he considered to be in order. No, sir; I cannot believe that the Speaker deliberately and maliciously gave me faulty advice in order later to be able to rule the motion out of order. It was a matter he took too seriously to play ducks and drakes with on any cynical basis of that sort.
Now, we have to seek for some other reason. The only reason that comes to my mind, Mr. Speaker, is that in those fateful hours between 10 o'clock on the night of May 31 and 11 o'clock on the morning of June 1 the Speaker of this house must have been subjected to persuasion, to pressure, to evil counsel of some sort to persuade him to declare out of order a motion which he himself had accepted, had helped to draft, and which he had indicated was definitely in order.
It is not possible, of course, Mr. Speaker, for us to know who can have given that advice; but that such advice must have been given is I think incontrovertible. And while we cannot know who gave that advice we do know of people in a position to give that advice, and we do know of people to whom the implementation of such advice would have been of great advantage.

speechtext:
I am not coming to McCarthy at all; I am coming to a few other things. The Speaker of the Canadian House of Commons occupies a precarious position of eminence from which at the end of the life of parliament he has to step down. There are a number of positions of dignity and honour, positions in which he can hope to find further opportunities for public service. All those positions are within the power of the government of the day to grant or to withhold.
It has been suggested that Mr. Speaker proceeded to reverse a mistake he had made. I submit, sir, that if that is true with regard to other actions he took on that occasion, the action of listening to the point of order of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, it is distinctly not the case with regard to this motion, because if you will recall he handled the two situations in an entirely different manner. His decision with regard to my motion was not included as a part of
House of Commons
the mistake he sought to rectify by placing a proposition before this house. It is an entirely different action. He took the action of ruling it out of order. Somewhere, at some time, he was persuaded that his action of the night before in accepting and helping to draft my motion had been out of order. Somehow he was persuaded that the motion itself was out of order.
I find it difficult to believe, sir, that among his colleagues on the other side of the house the Speaker of the House of Commons found someone more versed in the procedure of this chamber than himself, in the light of the fact that with the rather doubtful exception of the Minister of Finance no member of the cabinet has risen through all this time to oppose the points of order raised from the opposition. This would lead me and I think anyone else to the conclusion that there is not anyone on the other side of the house now capable of disputing the points of order raised from this side.
I see that the Minister of Finance laughs. If by his laughter he means that he or others are so capable, then I say it was a contemptible thing for the government of the day to allow the Speaker of this house to deal by himself with the points of order that were raised continually from this side of the house, to place him in the impossible position not of being the judge as between two opposing sides but having to take up the arguments presented by one side. I am still of the opinion, sir, that there is not anyone on that side of the house sufficiently versed in procedure to be able to give valid and honest advice to the Speaker of this house to cause him to reverse a considered decision that he had made.
I have been puzzled, as have many other hon. members of this house, by the strange procedural activities of this government during the whole presentation of the pipe-lines bill to the house. I have wondered why they apparently took great thought to select the most difficult ways in which to get this measure through. The first sample, of course, was when quite out of order they placed a second resolution on the order paper while one dealing with the same subject was already there. That was a totally unnecessary proceeding. I recall that at that time the government received advice from my hon. friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as to how they could emerge from the difficulty they had themselves created.
I suggest to you that we have to look further for a solution to this strange problem, and it is a strange problem, a strange problem of a government so inept that it is unable to get its measures through the House

House of Commons
of Commons within the accepted rules of this house. I would suggest to you that perhaps an explanation can be found in the constitution of the present administration. I think it is no accident that the government that has involved itself in a most fantastic tangle of procedure, that has been driven in the course of that tangle to utterly destroy the most notable Speaker this house has seen for decades. It is not an accident that many of the members of that administration have stepped right into cabinet positions without any experience in parliamentary life.
I would suggest to you that this has been the root cause of the trouble through which we have been going the last few years, and the last few days in particular. When one looks at the front treasury benches he finds that with two exceptions no minister has sat on the floor of this house as a private member, and no minister at all has sat on the floor of this house as a member in opposition. This creates a very grave situation for parliament. I am not attempting to deny that eminent university presidents, distinguished corporation lawyers and higher civil servants are men of great ability. They are possibly of greater ability than other men who could be found within the membership of the Liberal party; but their abilities were not the abilities of parliamentarians because there is only one place in which a man can qualify for this difficult business of parliamentary life, and that is in the ranks of parliament itself.
I would suggest that this growing habit on the part of this administration of bringing in from outside the ranks of parliament cabinet ministers without parliamentary experience is destroying the very roots of parliament. This institution has several functions to perform. It is not merely an institution for the passing of legislation by the existing government, it is the developing ground for competent parliamentary leadership.
When we have a party-and I address this to the rank and file of the Liberal party- which has acquiesced in this practice, it has been acquiescing in the degradation of parliament because these men, eminent as they are, lack one thing. They are men who have not, like the Minister of Finance and like the Minister of National Health and Welfare, been prepared in their earlier years to take the grave risks involved in embarking upon a political career. On the other hand, they have sought their eminence in other fields and later come to crown it with political eminence. That is a most dangerous precedent and practice for parliament to follow, when parliament should be composed of ordinary men and women representing ordinary men and women throughout the nation.

From the ranks of the membership must come those men who have developed their capacities and their abilities to use the procedures and rules of parliament in order to effect their policies. I can understand that the minister of external affairs may perhaps feel badly about my comments, but I want to say to him that the very qualities which made him a valuable servant of the people in the civil service are not qualities that make him valuable in the House of Commons when it comes to dealing with difficult parliamentary situations. He never had to face them during his earlier career.
It will not be until we get back to the original purposes of parliament, to the original proceedings and traditions of parliament, that we shall avoid the sort of tragic mess into which we got last week. I think it is a damning indictment of a government with an overwhelming majority that it should have been unable to devise means of using the regular procedures of this house to effect the passage of their legislation. It is an admission of total ineptitude and failure as leaders of the Canadian parliament that they had to take recourse to breaches of the rules which have led to this unhappy debate during these last two days. It is particularly tragic that a man who had earned not only the respect of this parliament but the respect of the nation should have been made the victim of the ineptitude of this government, and ineptitude it was, as I think every member of it now recognizes in his secret heart.
I would suggest that there is no solution to be found in the mere passing or rejection of the motion before us. As the Minister of Finance has said, when it comes to a vote the matter will be decided on party lines and the vote will mean nothing. A vote will not in any way obliterate the sad fact that a large minority in this house has had its confidence in the impartiality of the Chair destroyed by the ineptitude and folly of the present administration.
I notice that some members of the cabinet are so little seized of the seriousness of the crime they have committed as to smile smugly about this situation. It is nothing to smile about, it is something that has to be cleared up. I am not making any empty suggestion when I suggest to the Prime Minister that he has something to retrieve. I am not alone in my view that he has failed sadly this parliament and this country in these last strenuous and trying days.
I imagine he has read the newspapers. I imagine he realizes that the people of Canada are disappointed that they had hoped he could master the art of using parliamentary procedures, that they hoped he could retain

control of the democratic processes of this country. I suggest to him that, having failed to do so, there is only one course open to him, the course of appealing to the people and allowing them to judge. I say this in no boastful way at all. I am not at all sure that I would come back here after another election; far from it. I think it is quite possible that I might be left at home, but I would rather be left at home than continue in the unhappy situation in which we are today.
Despite the words that have been said on this side of the house in, I think, all sincerity that this situation is not going to be allowed to interfere with the personal friendships that have been developed here, I am afraid that is a too optimistic point of view and that it is going to take a long time for the resentments, the rancours and the dis-illusionments that have been created over the last week or so to finally disappear. The first and essential step for clearing the air is that the twenty-second parliament of Canada should come to an end at the earliest possible moment.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that whatever may have happened in the house during the past few days we will all agree that the discussion of this particular motion has been approached by every hon. member almost throughout in a spirit at least of seemingly objective manner. I paid particular attention to the speech delivered tonight by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I followed with interest the speech just delivered by the hon. member for Nanaimo and the speech of the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, but I paid special attention to the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
He began his remarks by saying that this discussion of the motion before the house caused him to have a heavy heart. I am sure he used a phrase that most hon. gentlemen could, with justification repeat. He reminded us that there was no friendship in this house that he cherished as much as his friendship with Mr. Speaker. He told us that there was never a Speaker in this house whose industry was as great, that there never was a Speaker with knowledge of our procedures and the procedures of free parliaments over the course of the centuries as great, as precise and as mature.
Then he said that he hoped that his friendship with the Speaker would be maintained
House of Comvions
and would continue. Only a man who was lacking in the elements of civility would deny that that was a legitimate hope. I too hope that the friendship which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had with Mr. Speaker will be maintained, for I suppose that no one in the whole time I have been a member of the House of Commons, now almost 21 years, has enjoyed in his relations in this house as great a measure of cordial relationship with the presiding officer as the member for Winnipeg North Centre. On many occasions his enthusiasm with respect to his interest in the rules of the house would cause him, not improperly, after the Speaker's ruling had been made, to go to the Speaker's chair and presumably in a spirit of academic interest, which is understandable, discuss with Mr. Speaker the wisdom or lack of wisdom in a particular decision. The hon. gentleman himself and only he has the control over whether or not the friendship of which he has spoken tonight shall be maintained.
The hon. member went on then and said, and I use his words, that no one will deny that Mr. Speaker has done a good job. Then he raised his voice and said with emotion: "No one ever in my time in this house has done a better job." Then he went on and pointed out that he had corrected the Minister of Finance, that there had only been two appeals from Mr. Speaker's rulings and that on one occasion the party which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre supports had, if I understood him correctly, refused to join in voting against the Speaker's ruling. Then my hon. friend concluded, "No wonder I say that Mr. Speaker has had in this house a remarkable performance."
I calculated by the clock the time that my hon. friend spent on Mr. Speaker's admirable qualities. In over two-thirds of the time he spoke the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said more things by way of' confirmation of the validity of the performance of the Speaker than any other member, and we can only conclude from what he has said that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, up until a very few days ago, was firmly of the view that within his experience this house has had no better Speaker.

speechtext:
de Grace):
1.	By provinces, how many sufferers from diabetes are there in Canada?
2.	How many of these are hospitalized?
3.	Is the government currently engaged in any activities designed directly to assist Canadian diabetics?
4.	If so, of what nature?
5.	Are any further measures to assist Canadian diabetics currently under consideration?
6.	If so, of what nature?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
1.	There is no accurate gauge of the number of diabetics in Canada. According to preliminary estimates based on Canada's sickness survey, population basis 13,000,000, there are about 40,000 known diabetics; however, medical experience has shown that for every reported case, there are about three unreported cases.
2.	There are approximately 8,500 hospital admissions per year in Canada of patients requiring treatment for diabetes.
3.	Yes.
4.	Federal assistance totalling more than $65,000 has been provided under the national health program to support research and surveys on the detection of diabetes. Research in diabetic problems is being supported at present at the University of Western Ontario and at Queen's University.
The Food and Drugs Act provides that all insulin preparations must meet the standards set forth in the food and drug regulations. In addition, the conditions under which these preparations are manufactured are constantly reviewed by the food and drug inspectors. The regulations also provide for specific labelling requirements to prevent confusion regarding the potency and the use of each preparation.
The advertisement to the general public of any preparation for the prevention or treatment of diabetes is prohibited by the act, thus preventing the exposure of diabetics to useless or harmful preparations.
The food and drug regulations also require informative labelling of special food products sold for persons on sugar-restricted diets.
5 and 6. The Department of National Health and Welfare will continue to give the most careful consideration to any projects designed
to assist Canadian diabetics when submitted by the provinces under the national health program.

URBAN AIR POLLUTION
speechtext:
Is the Department of National Health and Welfare taking any part in the solution of the urban air pollution problem?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
1. Yes. The Department of National Health and Welfare has assisted the international joint commission for several years in the investigation of the problem of air pollution in the Windsor-Detroit area in accordance with the terms of the reference of January, 1949, between Canada and the United States. A two-year epidemiological study of sickness experience of selected groups of the population in high and low pollution areas of Windsor, and in small country towns of southern Ontario, was carried out from 1953 to 1955. Other aspects of this investigation of the urban air pollution problem have dealt with the nature and concentration of contaminants in the environment, the influence of meteorological factors, the problem of smoke emission from great lakes vessel traffic on the Detroit river and its control, and the effects on vegetation. A final report on the above reference is being prepared this year.
Since January 1, 1956, this department has also undertaken certain responsibilities in this field with the appointment of a consultant, atmospheric pollution services, who is also the chairman of the Canadian section of a technical advisory board to the international joint commission. Requests for advisory services from the provinces and other governmental agencies have been coming forward on an increasing scale. The following is an outline of these activities:
(a)	The pollution of the air from oil refinery operations involving the emission of toxic substances such as hydrogen sulphide, mercaptans, phenols, and other odoriferous compounds.
(b)	The control of emissions of fluorides, oxides of nitrogen and sulphur dioxide from contemplated operations of a new phosphate fertilizer and nitro-chemical plant.
(c)	The analysis and control of diesel exhaust gas fumes from engine-operated equipment in underground and mining operations.
(d)	At the request of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada a complete revision has been undertaken of regulations and orders dealing with

control of atmospheric pollution from railroad operations of companies subject to the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada.
The epidemiological and occupational health divisions of the Department of National Health and Welfare are collaborating in a study of atmospheric pollution levels and their possible effects on the health of aged hospital patients in the Ottawa area.
The laboratory services of the occupational health division are conducting laboratory research directed towards the study of the biological effects of various toxic gases and
Questions
aerosols, including the effects of substances found in contaminated urban atmospheres. The laboratory services have also studied for several years the problem of atmospheric pollution from gold refining operations in the Yellowknife area.
Consideration is being given to the possibility of the establishment of a national network of sampling stations for the measurement of atmospheric contamination levels in urban areas of Canada in co-operation with provincial departments of health, municipal air pollution control officials and certain federal departments.
